purpose: Ranked, nonredundant embodied sky-orientation factoids for Oracle of Relphi. Rank 1 is most worthy to share.
ranking_policy: Prioritize usable embodied conversions, surprising insight, factual reliability, and novelty. Compare new entries with existing ones before adding; avoid duplicate principles and near-identical variations. Re-rank after every addition. Earlier historical selections are preserved; new daily additions must be genuinely distinct.

factoids.title: The Moon travels about one Moon-width per hour
factoids.fact: Relative to the background stars, the Moon advances about 0.55° per hour, roughly its apparent half-degree diameter.
factoids.application: Watch its position against nearby stars change over a few hours.
factoids.caveat: Its speed and apparent size vary; compare against stars rather than the horizon.

factoids.title: Polaris measures your northern latitude
factoids.fact: In the Northern Hemisphere, Polaris's altitude above a level northern horizon is approximately your latitude north.
factoids.application: Estimate latitude by measuring the North Star's height with a hand or angular ruler.
factoids.caveat: Polaris is not exactly at the celestial pole; local horizon obstructions can interfere.

factoids.title: A ruler becomes a celestial protractor
factoids.fact: Hold a ruler 57.3 cm (22.6 in) from your eye: 1 cm spans about 1° and 1 mm spans about 6′.
factoids.application: Measure small apparent separations directly instead of guessing finger widths.
factoids.caveat: Hold it perpendicular to your line of sight; apparent angular separation is not necessarily ecliptic longitude separation.

factoids.title: The Sun advances two Sun-widths a day
factoids.fact: The Sun shifts roughly 1° eastward along the ecliptic each day, about twice its apparent half-degree diameter.
factoids.application: Picture the Sun taking roughly one month to cross a 30° zodiac sign.
factoids.caveat: This is relative to background stars and cannot be watched directly beside the Sun; orbital speed varies.

factoids.title: The stars run four minutes ahead each night
factoids.fact: At the same clock time on successive nights, the background stars appear about 1° farther west, or reach a given position about four minutes earlier.
factoids.application: Anticipate seasonal constellation changes: roughly two hours earlier after a month.
factoids.caveat: Approximate because a sidereal day is 23 h 56 min 4 s; use a fixed observing location and solar clock time.

factoids.title: Venus cannot reach a solar sextile
factoids.fact: Seen from Earth, Venus stays within about 47° of the Sun, so it cannot form a 60° geocentric longitude separation from the Sun.
factoids.application: Look for Venus within roughly five fist-widths of the sunset or sunrise Sun's direction; understand why some Sun–Venus aspects never occur.
factoids.caveat: Maximum elongation varies; never look toward the Sun with optical instruments.

factoids.title: A fist is ten degrees of sky
factoids.fact: Your clenched fist at arm's length spans about 10° of sky, so three fists approximate one 30° zodiac sign.
factoids.caveat: Individual anatomy and arm length affect the calibration.

factoids.title: An equinox shadow can reveal latitude
factoids.fact: At true solar noon near an equinox, the Sun's altitude is approximately 90° minus the magnitude of your latitude; a vertical stick and its shadow reveal that altitude.
factoids.application: Measure the stick's height and shadow length to estimate your latitude.
factoids.caveat: Use level ground and true solar noon; this simple relation assumes a location where the Sun culminates toward the equator and ignores refraction.

factoids.title: The noon Sun swings about 47° between solstices
factoids.fact: At mid-northern and mid-southern latitudes, the Sun's noon altitude changes by about 46.9° between the June and December solstices, twice Earth's 23.44° axial tilt.
factoids.application: Observe the seasonal change in the Sun's height and your noon shadow.
factoids.caveat: The simple altitude swing applies where the Sun remains on the same side of the zenith at culmination.

factoids.title: A pinky is about one degree
factoids.fact: The width of your little finger at arm's length is roughly 1°; the Moon's apparent diameter is about half that.
factoids.application: Use your body to visualize one-degree aspect orbs.
factoids.caveat: Hand dimensions vary, and chart longitude differences do not always equal visual sky separation.

factoids.title: One hour of sky rotation is fifteen degrees
factoids.fact: Earth's rotation makes the stellar sky turn about 15° per hour, or roughly half a zodiac sign.
factoids.application: Connect a familiar hour of time with an angular turn of the sky.
factoids.caveat: This is rotation about the celestial pole; actual apparent displacement on the sky depends on declination.

factoids.title: One minute of latitude is roughly one nautical mile
factoids.fact: One arcminute of latitude on Earth spans about one nautical mile (1.852 km), so a degree spans roughly 60 nautical miles.
factoids.application: Connect the arcminutes of coordinates with distances you could travel north or south.
factoids.caveat: The length of a minute of latitude varies slightly with latitude because Earth is not spherical.

factoids.title: A noon shadow marks the meridian
factoids.fact: At true solar noon, a vertical stick's shadow lies along the local north–south line.
factoids.application: Find a local cardinal axis using only sunlight and a vertical stick.
factoids.caveat: The shadow may point north or south; solar noon usually differs from 12:00 civil time.

factoids.title: Two motions carry the Moon in opposite directions
factoids.fact: The stellar sky turns west at about 15° per hour while the Moon advances east relative to stars at about 0.55° per hour.
factoids.application: Compare the Moon to a nearby star to distinguish Earth's rotation from lunar orbital motion.
factoids.caveat: This synthesizes two existing rules; the apparent path across the horizon varies with sky position.
